blocks.text: Capture an object's internal state in an opaque snapshot so it can be restored later.

The **originator** creates a **memento** of its own state and later restores itself from one. A **caretaker** stores mementos, for example in an undo stack, but cannot read or change them. Encapsulation holds: only the originator understands the snapshot's contents.

items: **Caretaker:** decides when to save and restore, never inspects.

blocks.text: Typical uses are undo, checkpoints and transactional rollback of in-memory state.

walkthrough.note: `Memento` is an empty public marker. The real snapshot is a private record, so only `Editor` can read its fields. Encapsulation is enforced by the compiler.
The caretaker stores opaque `Memento` values on a stack. It has no way to look inside, edit or fabricate a snapshot.
Snapshots are taken before each change. `save()` copies the text into an immutable `String`, so later typing cannot corrupt a stored memento.
Restoring pops the latest snapshot and the editor rebuilds its own state from it. Each `pop` steps one checkpoint back.

blocks.text: Rolling back a failed bulk edit in a diagram editor.

A user applies an auto-layout to a diagram with 2,000 shapes. The layout engine mutates positions in place and may fail halfway. Before running it, the editor takes a snapshot of positions and styles. On failure or on Ctrl-Z, it restores from the snapshot. Stored snapshots are compact (positions only), and the history panel can list them without understanding their contents.
Payoff: atomic, in-memory rollback with no change to the layout engine and no public setters on the diagram's internals.

lists.title: Use when
items: You need undo, checkpoints or rollback of an object's state.
Exposing the state through getters would break encapsulation.
State is small enough, or copy-on-write, to snapshot cheaply.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: State is huge and changes by small deltas: store the delta instead.
The object already is immutable; keep the old reference.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Shallow copies: mutable fields shared with the live object corrupt the snapshot.
Unbounded history exhausts memory; cap it or compact.
Mementos that hold external resources (files, connections) cannot be restored faithfully.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: A nested private record is a compact, immutable memento.
With immutable state, the memento is the previous value itself: no pattern needed.

rows.difference: Undo with Command stores the inverse operation, which is cheap in memory. Memento stores the state itself, which is simpler when inverses are hard. Editors often mix both.
Both copy state. Prototype produces a new live object to use; a memento is an opaque snapshot that is only ever fed back to its originator.
An iterator can save its position as a memento so a traversal can be resumed or rewound.
Event sourcing rebuilds state from the full history of events, with snapshots as an optimization. Memento keeps only chosen snapshots.
State changes behavior with the object's mode. Memento does not change behavior; it saves data to return to later.

entries.name: java.io.Serializable
entries.detail: Serialization turns an object into an opaque byte snapshot that can be restored later; `ObjectOutputStream` writes it and `ObjectInputStream` reads it.

entries.name: javax.swing.undo.UndoManager
entries.detail: Swing's undo framework stores `UndoableEdit`s that restore a document's earlier state.

entries.name: Persistence context loaded state
entries.detail: Hibernate keeps a snapshot of an entity's loaded state to detect dirty fields at flush.

entries.name: Commit
entries.detail: Each commit is an immutable snapshot of the working tree to which you can restore.

options.why: The object hands out an opaque copy of its state and rebuilds itself from it later.
Nothing creates a new live canvas; the copy is only fed back to the same object.
No operation is being encapsulated or reversed; state, not an action, is stored.
Behavior does not vary with a mode; the snapshot is data.

exercises.scenario: A spreadsheet needs multi-level undo. Cell state is private and mutated through many operations, some hard to invert, such as sort and paste with formatting. Sheets are small enough to copy.

options.why: Snapshots restore state regardless of how it was mutated, without exposing the cells' internals.
Needs an inverse for every operation, which is difficult for sort and paste here.
Cloning produces new live objects; the need is restoring one object to an earlier state.
Notifying listeners of changes does not let you return to a prior state.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that breaks the Memento pattern.
lines: private final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
exercises.explanation: The snapshot holds a reference to the live list, so later `add` calls change the saved state and `restore` even clears its own source. Save a copy: `new Snapshot(List.copyOf(lines))`.
Create the store, snapshot before mutating, mutate, then restore from the snapshot. Saving after the edit would capture the wrong state.

template: final class Editor { interface Memento {} void type(String s) {}
Memento save() { return new Memento() {}; } void restore(Memento m) {} }

exercises.prompt: Explain Memento in your own words: who creates snapshots, who stores them, and why it preserves encapsulation.

modelAnswer.text: The originator creates an opaque snapshot of its own state and can restore itself from one. A caretaker stores snapshots, such as an undo stack, but cannot read them, so the originator's internals stay private. Snapshots must be immutable copies, not references into live state.

keyPoints: Caretaker stores them without looking inside
Command undo stores operations; Memento stores state
